newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African ex-police question de Klerk's innocence.
newsitem.headline: S.African ex-police question de Klerk's innocence.

text.p: Former South African secret police came forward on Monday to expose apartheid-era murders of black activists and said they doubted ex-president F.W. de Klerk's claims of clean hands.
The five, among them a brigadier who commanded a notorious secret police unit that spawned a death squad, hope to trade confessions for pardons from the "truth commission".
They have promised to give details of around 40 state- sponsored murders, bombings and assassinations during the 1980s and are expected to point fingers at their bosses.

"We call upon the previous government and our superiors to explain certain orders given to us about which we shall testify and to admit to authorising actions outside the normal processes of the law," they said in a statement.
They presented it to the commission's amnesty committee on Monday.
"We seriously doubt the statement made by Mr F.W. de Klerk...in the National Party submission to this commission," they added.
The white former president said in his submission presented to the truth commission earlier this year:

"I have never been part of any decision...authorising or instructing the commission of such gross violations of human rights. Nor did I individually, directly or indirectly ever suggest, order or authorise any such action."
The five said they regretted their actions, which they said were intended to prop up the white government and fight communism.
"We express compassion and regret to the families of those who have suffered as a consequence of our deeds," they said.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission has so far mainly heard testimony from blacks who suffered under apartheid, but few perpetrators have come clean.
The five said they supported de Klerk's National Party until 1994, when Nelson Mandela swept to power in South Africa's first all-race elections.
They said their ex-bosses had abandoned them.
"We have been deserted by the National Party and...thrown away in the gutter where we now have to take the responsibility on our shoulders to deal with our past."

The highest-ranking of the five is retired brigadier Jack Cronje, who commanded an infamous hit-squad unit near Pretoria in the early 1980s. He and another of the five face trial in connection with over two dozen murders.

Meanwhile in separate commission hearings in Cape Town, South Africa's current defence chief acknowledged that apartheid-era files were destroyed in the last years of apartheid to protect agents after the end of minority rule.

"In the view of not creating ill-feeling among the people of South Africa and also to protect lives, in the run-up to the elections, certain documents were destroyed that reflected names of agents and names of people that supplied information," General Georg Meiring said.
Meiring did not identify anyone who might have ordered the destruction of sensitive files and denied that instructions had come from de Klerk's government.
Earlier this month former defence minister Magnus Malan was acquitted of masterminding a death-squad massacre in 1987.
